title: Filing duties: AI use never displaces inquiry
desc: Applies existing certification and verification duties across participants, with sanctions depending on authority and contested mental-state standards.

kps.k: The central proposition is that AI-assisted filings remain subject to existing duties of reasonable inquiry and human verification.
kps.d: Park requires lawyers to read authorities and confirm their existence and validity; Coomer applies that duty directly to AI output. Rule 11 certifies reasonable inquiry, not infallibility, and preserves nonfrivolous arguments for changing the law. These materials frame fabricated citations as failures of professional responsibility rather than evidence that AI use itself is prohibited. They document sanctions incidents and legal standards, not model error rates.

qs.q: At the very least, the duties imposed by Rule 11 require that attorneys read, and thereby confirm the existence and validity of, the legal authorities on which they rely.
qs.a: Park v. Kim — Second Circuit opinion referring counsel to the Grievance Panel for a ChatGPT-fabricated citation · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: And because Rule 11(b) demands a reasonable  inquiry, “[a] litigant’s using AI and then failing to verify the accuracy of the results it yields  violates the litigant’s [Rule] 11 obligations.” Willis, 2025 WL 1224273, at *3.
qs.a: Coomer v. Lindell — Rule 11 Sanctions for AI-Generated Defective Citations ($3,000 Each, July 2025) and Repeat Sanction ($5,000, May 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Responsibility follows participation and certification, not simply who operated the AI tool.
kps.d: Withers finds violations by drafting lawyers and local signatories who admitted failing to review filings, despite the latter's ignorance of AI use. Wadsworth likewise rejects blind reliance on co-counsel and warns against authorising signatures without reasonable inquiry. Responsibility still requires individual assessment: Withers assigns greater responsibility to drafters, while the May 2026 Coomer proceedings discharge the show-cause order against DeMaster and Frankspeech after crediting their nonparticipation in the later response. Rule 11 ordinarily also makes firms jointly responsible, absent exceptional circumstances.

qs.q: The Court  finds that, through their own admissions, all four attorneys failed to verify the legal authorities  cited in their respective filings in violation of Rule 11.
qs.a: Withers v. City of Aberdeen — sanctions order: hallucinated citations by both sides, trial cancelled, two-year district bars · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: Thus, blind reliance on another attorney can  be an improper delegation of this duty and a violation of Rule 11.
qs.a: Wadsworth v. Walmart — sanctions where the hallucinated citations came from a law firm's internal AI platform · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Good intentions, plausible output and correct legal conclusions do not necessarily excuse fabricated supporting authorities.
kps.d: HoosierVac records Ramirez's explanation that excerpts appeared credible and that he did not know AI could invent cases, but applies an objective inquiry standard. Withers and Whiting reject the argument that genuine supporting law neutralises the harm from fabricated citations; Whiting says even one fake case can be sanctionable. Coomer rejects the claimed accidental filing of a defective version because counsel offered contradictory statements and lacked corroboration. These conclusions do not equate every legal mistake with misconduct: Mata expressly distinguishes merely incorrect statements and long-shot theories from sanctionable contentions.

qs.q: Ramirez did not  conduct any further research, nor did he make any attempt to verify the existence of the  generated citations.
qs.a: Mid Central Operating Engineers Health & Welfare Fund v. HoosierVac LLC — Report & Recommendation ($15,000) and Order ($6,000) Sanctioning Counsel for AI-Fabricated Citations in Three Briefs · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The principal doctrinal disagreement concerns the mental-state threshold for court-initiated sanctions.
kps.d: Withers, Billups and Wadsworth stress objective reasonableness and reject subjective good faith as sufficient protection. Mata, applying Second Circuit precedent, requires subjective bad faith for court-initiated sanctions in its circumstances, contrasting that route with adversary motions carrying a correction safe harbor. Cohen repeats that distinction, while Johnson expressly rejects interpreting the heightened court-initiated standard as requiring subjective bad faith. These positions should not become a single nationwide rule. Inherent-power sanctions also carry distinct bad-faith requirements; Cohen articulates a clear-and-convincing deliberate-deception threshold, and Lacey invokes the Ninth Circuit's specific-finding requirement.

qs.q: A  finding of subjective bad faith is not required to impose sanctions.
qs.a: Wadsworth v. Walmart — sanctions where the hallucinated citations came from a law firm's internal AI platform · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: When, as here, a court considers whether to impose sanctions sua sponte,  it “is akin to the court’s inherent power of contempt,” and, “like contempt, sua sponte sanctions  in those circumstances should issue only upon a finding of subjective bad faith.”  Muhammad,  732 F.3d at 108.
qs.a: Mata v. Avianca, Inc. — Opinion and Order on Sanctions · Regulators & courts · 2023

kps.k: Courts must identify an applicable sanctions mechanism rather than assume Rule 11 governs every fabricated citation.
kps.d: Rule 11 excludes discovery matters under Rules 26–37. Johnson therefore declines to apply it to the discovery motions at issue and identifies a gap because the discovery rules did not address those false legal statements. In Lacey, an opposing submission—not a judicial finding—argues that the contemplated pleading sanctions lack the required violation of a discovery order. Cohen explains that civil Rule 11 does not govern its criminal proceeding. Whiting instead discusses appellate obligations under Rule 38. Inherent authority and professional discipline remain possible alternatives, but their separate prerequisites matter.

qs.q: This rule does not apply to disclosures and discovery requests, responses, objections, and motions under Rules [26](/rules/frcp/rule_26) through [37](/rules/frcp/rule_37).
qs.a: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 — Signing Pleadings, Motions, and Other Papers; Representations to the Court; Sanctions (rule text with Advisory Committee Notes) · Regulators & courts · 2007

qs.a: Johnson v. Dunn — Sanctions Opinion Against Butler Snow Attorneys for AI-Hallucinated Citations · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Sanctions remain discretionary, proportionate and procedurally constrained even after a violation is established.
kps.d: The current rule limits sanctions to sufficient deterrence, requires notice and an opportunity to respond, and requires courts to explain their orders. Party motions generally provide 21 days to withdraw or correct before filing; court-initiated show-cause proceedings follow a separate route. Fee awards require the specified motion, deterrence and direct-causation conditions, while represented parties receive protection from monetary sanctions for legal contentions. The Advisory Committee warns against using sanctions to intimidate opponents or litigate minor errors. Historical mandatory-sanction language should not displace the current discretionary text.

qs.q: (1) In General.* If, after notice and a reasonable opportunity to respond, the court determines that Rule 11(b) has been violated, the court may impose an appropriate sanction on any attorney, law firm, or party that violated the rule or is responsible for the violation.
qs.a: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 — Signing Pleadings, Motions, and Other Papers; Representations to the Court; Sanctions (rule text with Advisory Committee Notes) · Regulators & courts · 2007

qs.q: The motion must be served under [Rule 5](/rules/frcp/rule_5), but it must not be filed or be presented to the court if the challenged paper, claim, defense, contention, or denial is withdrawn or appropriately corrected within 21 days after service or within another time the court sets.
qs.a: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 — Signing Pleadings, Motions, and Other Papers; Representations to the Court; Sanctions (rule text with Advisory Committee Notes) · Regulators & courts · 2007

kps.k: Correction, candor and preventive safeguards affect sanctions, while repetition and continued advocacy increase exposure.
kps.d: The signing-time inquiry does not exhaust responsibility: Rule 11 also covers later advocacy of positions known to lack merit, and state candor duties require correction of knowing material falsehoods. Ferris finds a violation where false citations continued after notice. Withers weighs corrective action against a pattern across filings. Wadsworth credits employee training and a new independent-verification acknowledgement when declining additional firm sanctions. HoosierVac reports remedial education and assurances about products, but does not establish those assurances' reliability. Practical implications include checking authorities before filing, controlling signature permissions, correcting discovered errors and implementing verification procedures.

qs.q: However, a litigant's obligations with respect to the contents of these papers are not measured solely as of the time they are filed with or submitted to the court, but include reaffirming to the court and advocating positions contained in those pleadings and motions after learning that they cease to have any merit.
qs.a: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 — Signing Pleadings, Motions, and Other Papers; Representations to the Court; Sanctions (rule text with Advisory Committee Notes) · Regulators & courts · 2007

qs.q: Ferris violated Rule 11 by submitting false citations to the Court—first, in his complaint; then, after being put on notice by Defendant, in his subsequent filings.
qs.a: Ferris v. Amazon.com Services, LLC — Order on AI-Fabricated Citations by a Pro Se Litigant (N.D. Miss.) · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The policy debate asks whether existing accountability rules suffice or need AI-specific reinforcement.
kps.d: A January 2024 comment on the Fifth Circuit proposal argues that an additional AI-use certification would duplicate existing signature duties and sanctions powers; the supplied excerpt does not establish the court's subsequent reasoning. Johnson calls for effective preventive measures, while Wadsworth illustrates firm-level safeguards without a categorical AI ban. Withers supplies a concrete litigation consequence: the court stayed the case and cancelled the scheduled trial. These materials support an enforcement-and-governance debate, not a demonstrated conclusion that certifications or sanctions reduce hallucinations. Several excerpts omit final dispositions, so source-label fines, practice bars and tentative dismissal language should not be treated as established outcomes.

qs.q: An additional, AI-specific order requiring another certification subject to the threat of sanctions would be redundant.
qs.a: Fifth Circuit proposed Rule 32.3 and Form 6 (AI-use certification): notice, public comments, and the court's June 2024 decision not to adopt · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The curated regulators, courts and professional-body materials accept the principal proposition that AI assistance does not displace existing duties of reasonable inquiry, verification and candour. They materially develop it by specifying that responsibility follows signing, drafting, authorising a signature and later advocacy—not merely operation of the AI tool—and can therefore extend to co-counsel and firms while remaining participation-specific. They also supply a detailed enforcement architecture: the court must identify the applicable authority; Rule 11 does not govern every procedural setting; inherent authority and other mechanisms have distinct prerequisites; and sanctions remain discretionary, procedurally safeguarded and proportionate to deterrence. Material internal variation concerns the mental-state threshold for court-initiated sanctions: some decisions apply objective reasonableness and reject good faith as a defence, while Second Circuit authorities require subjective bad faith in relevant sua sponte proceedings, and inherent-power sanctions carry separate bad-faith standards. Policy views also differ over whether existing rules suffice: one public comment treats AI-specific certification as redundant, whereas other judicial material calls for preventive measures and firm-level verification controls. These differences refine implementation rather than undermine the shared verification proposition. One fragment, Fletcher, is too incomplete to establish a position and addresses only conduct-linked fee recovery.

vlens.an: The academia-and-research sources support the principal proposition that AI-assisted court filings remain governed by existing duties of reasonable inquiry and human verification. Both frame Rule 11 as attaching responsibility to the lawyer’s presentation of a filing, rather than allowing reliance on a tool to displace counsel’s obligation to ensure factual and legal support. The Legal Ethics of Generative AI applies that framework directly to generative AI and cites a sanctions incident involving fictitious ChatGPT-generated citations. Who Should Regulate Lawyers? supplies the broader doctrinal foundation: filing certification can supplement professional discipline by enforcing factual grounding, legal justification and proper purpose. There is some internal variation in emphasis, but not direction: the former is AI-specific and incident-based, whereas the latter predates generative AI and addresses Rule 11 as a general lawyer-regulation mechanism. Neither source materially develops the synthesis’s more contested issues, including responsibility among multiple participants, mental-state thresholds, the limits of Rule 11’s coverage, or sanctions procedure and proportionality. Because the evidence accepts the proposition without adding a substantial new doctrinal or practical framework, the appropriate position is Supports rather than Builds on.

elens.an: The pre-2015 foundations support the proposition by establishing a tool-neutral accountability framework: counsel’s presentation or later advocacy of a court paper certifies a reasonable inquiry into its factual and legal basis, and counsel must read the paper before submission. AI is not discussed, so these sources do not independently establish what AI-specific verification entails; rather, they supply the pre-existing duties that later authorities apply to AI-assisted filings. The principal internal variation is emphasis, not direction. Rule 11 and its Advisory Committee Notes provide the governing duties, continuing responsibility, procedural safeguards, and proportionate sanctions limits. “Who Should Regulate Lawyers?” focuses on the 1983 rule’s signature-based warranty and reports a commentator’s broader claim that federal-court enforcement could supplement gaps in state professional discipline. Its account reflects the historical 1983 formulation and should not displace the current rule’s discretionary, procedurally bounded sanctions regime. These are two curated foundational sources, so their agreement is not evidence of prevalence among pre-2015 commentators.

The curated 2023–2024 sources collectively accept the proposition that using generative AI does not displace lawyers’ existing duties of reasonable inquiry, verification and candour. Park states the baseline most directly: counsel must read cited authorities and confirm their existence and validity. Mata and the legal-ethics source reinforce that Rule 11 governs AI-assisted filings without making AI use itself prohibited or treating every legal error as sanctionable. The period materially develops the proposition by specifying how accountability operates: Mata distinguishes ordinary error from sanctionable misconduct, requires subjective bad faith for court-initiated Rule 11 sanctions in its Second Circuit setting, and stresses restrained, deterrence-focused remedies; Cohen further separates inherent authority, Section 1927 and civil Rule 11, including Rule 11’s inapplicability in a criminal proceeding. The principal internal variation is therefore doctrinal and policy-oriented rather than opposition to verification: the cases qualify sanctions by the applicable authority, procedural route and mental-state threshold, while the January 2024 comment argues that existing signature and sanctions rules make an additional AI-specific certification redundant. These sources support the cluster’s core while adding material detail about sanctions mechanisms, limits and the debate over AI-specific reinforcement; they do not establish model error rates or the effectiveness of certification requirements.

qs.q: At the very least, the duties imposed by Rule 11 require that attorneys read, and thereby confirm the existence and validity of, the legal authorities on which they rely.

elens.an: The curated 2025 materials support the synthesis’s principal proposition that using AI does not displace existing duties of reasonable inquiry and human verification. Their common rationale is doctrinal rather than empirical: Rule 11 and related professional duties attach to filing, signing, authorising a signature and later advocacy, while fabricated or unverified authorities cannot be justified merely because the output appeared credible, counsel acted without malice or another lawyer operated the AI. The sources also consistently treat sanctions as deterrent, discretionary and proportionate rather than as automatic punishment or a prohibition on AI use. Material variation concerns implementation and sanctions authority, not the underlying verification duty. Wadsworth develops personal, nondelegable responsibility and credits a firm-level independent-verification safeguard; Coomer expressly applies reasonable inquiry to AI results and assesses responsibility by participation; Ferris emphasizes repetition after notice; and HoosierVac and Billups apply objective reasonableness despite claimed good faith. Lacey and Johnson place greater emphasis on mechanism-specific limits: inherent-authority sanctions require an appropriate bad-faith finding, and Johnson identifies discovery motions to which Rule 11 does not apply. The sources also differ over whether subjective bad faith is required in particular court-initiated proceedings, but that disagreement does not undermine their shared acceptance of the filing and verification duties themselves. One supplied Coomer record includes May 2026 proceedings, so that later material should not be treated as evidence about the 2025 period itself.

qs.q: And because Rule 11(b) demands a reasonable  inquiry, “[a] litigant’s using AI and then failing to verify the accuracy of the results it yields  violates the litigant’s [Rule] 11 obligations.” Willis, 2025 WL 1224273, at *3.
qs.a: Coomer v. Lindell — Rule 11 Sanctions for AI-Generated Defective Citations ($3,000 Each, July 2025) and Repeat Sanction ($5,000, May 2026) · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2026 sources collectively accept the principal proposition that AI assistance or outsourced drafting does not displace existing duties of reasonable inquiry and human verification. They materially develop it by allocating responsibility across the workflow: Withers applies Rule 11 to both lawyers who used AI and local signatories who failed to review filings, while assigning greater responsibility to the drafters. Whiting extends the same logic to appellate advocacy under Rule 38, holding that genuine law or a correct legal conclusion does not neutralise fabricated citations and that even one fake case may be sanctionable. The Cassata compilation reinforces that the signing attorney remains accountable when drafting is outsourced to a provider, but also shows material variation in consequences: sanctions ranged from financial and professional measures to warnings or no monetary sanction, with disclosure, remediation and bad faith affecting outcomes. Fletcher is consistent with the synthesis’s proportionality and direct-causation constraints, but its fragmented text neither establishes the court’s endorsement nor addresses AI use or verification, so it does not independently establish a position on the central proposition. Overall, this period strengthens the proposition through concrete applications across participants and procedural settings, while preserving individualized, authority-specific sanction analysis rather than treating every verification failure identically.
